text:
**Education in Finland** consists of a nine-year comprehensive school (peruskoulu/ground school) from grades 1 to 9, with compulsory education expanded to include upper secondary education (lukio/gymnasium or ammattikoulu/vocational school) from age 15 onward. The system is non-selective, with no "gifted" programs; instead, advanced students support those who struggle. Small class sizes (under 20 students) and minimal homework promote student achievement, especially in science. Students learn two languages beyond their native tongue, and are exposed to arts, music, and practical skills. Schools offer free meals, books, and trips, and health care is provided.
Upper secondary education is now compulsory (since 2021), with students choosing between academic (leading to university) or vocational tracks. Advanced curricula in academic schools exist in mathematics, with a national exam grading students on a 4–10 scale. Teachers are fully unionized, follow state guidelines, and have autonomy in instruction.
Tertiary education includes traditional universities (focusing on research) and universities of applied sciences (focusing on practical, work-oriented education). Admission is merit-based, transparent, and objective, with no application essays or bias. Bachelor's degrees take 3–4 years, with master's degrees requiring further study.
Adult education is accessible through "free education" institutes (e.g., kansalaisopisto), offering non-degree, personality-development courses. The national curriculum emphasizes play-based, phenomenon-based learning, fostering creativity, collaboration, and critical thinking. Finnish education abroad includes official Suomi-koulut schools and "Finnish-style" private schools inspired by its model. Finland promotes digital learning and AI literacy, with free online AI courses available to all. The system is known for equity, well-being, and high student achievement.
